candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the serialized document fed to `XStream.fromXML(...)`/`unmarshal(...)` (XML by default via XppDriver; same semantics for the other drivers and for JSON-enabled drivers): root element name, nested element names, `class`/`resolves-to` attributes, `dynamic-proxy` `interface` values and the `handler class` attribute, and all property values written into the instantiated objects (e.g. the target/action fields of the chosen `InvocationHandler` and command arguments of the chosen target object).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for any in-repo mitigation: there is no `com.thoughtworks.xstream.security` package and no occurrence of `TypePermission`, `allowTypes`, `addPermission` or equivalent allow/deny logic in the snapshot (searches returned no matches); version 1.4.6 predates the 1.4.7 security framework. Verified `DefaultMapper.realClass` applies no package/type filter (only array-name initialization short-circuit and use of XStream's own classloader for `com.thoughtworks.xstream.*`). Verified the dynamic-proxy mapper and converters and the dangerous reflection/serialization converters are registered by default, not opt-in (XStream.java:562-595, 748-796). Checked the FAQ/changes/docs in the snapshot: no security section or untrusted-input warning exists that would indicate an assumed deployment mitigation. Confirmed the gadget requirement is effectively always satisfied because `java.beans.EventHandler` and `java.lang.ProcessBuilder` ship with the JDK. Also checked `FilePersistenceStrategy` filename escaping (no traversal found) and the DOM/StAX parser hardening gap (separate lower-impact lead). The RCE itself is not runtime-confirmed; no tests are present in the snapshot.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution with the privileges of the process performing unmarshalling (the classic CVE-2013-7285 outcome for pre-1.4.7 XStream), plus arbitrary object-graph manipulation and, via other gadget types, file/system access. Confidentiality, integrity and availability are all fully exposed when untrusted data is unmarshalled with this version.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The application passes attacker-influenced data to XStream 1.4.6's `fromXML`/`unmarshal` (the version offers no allowlist to enable; there is nothing to configure defensively). 2) A usable gadget exists on the application classpath; the canonical one is JDK-provided (`java.beans.EventHandler` implementing `InvocationHandler`, plus a command-execution target such as `java.lang.ProcessBuilder`), so a standard JRE satisfies this. 3) The classes named in the document must be loadable by XStream's classloader (JDK classes are). No elevated privileges of the attacker are required beyond the untrusted input channel.
candidates.root_cause: XStream 1.4.6 ships with no security framework and no permission/allowlist check anywhere in the unmarshalling pipeline. `TreeUnmarshaller.start()` derives the root type from the document's root element name and `HierarchicalStreams.readClassType()`/`AbstractReflectionConverter` derive nested types from `class`/`resolves-to` attributes; all of these are resolved by `DefaultMapper.realClass()` through `Class.forName(elementName, initialize, classLoader)` with no package or type restriction. The default mapper chain unconditionally installs `DynamicProxyMapper`, and the default converters include `DynamicProxyConverter`, `ReflectionConverter`, `SerializableConverter`, `ExternalizableConverter`, `TreeSetConverter` and `TreeMapConverter`. Consequently a document can (a) instantiate any class loadable by the configured classloader, (b) build a `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` over attacker-selected interfaces with an attacker-selected `InvocationHandler` class whose fields are populated from the document, and (c) trigger invocation of that handler during deserialization itself (collection converters call comparator/element methods while populating). A JDK `java.beans.EventHandler` handler populated with `target`/`action` fields therefore invokes an arbitrary target method (e.g. `ProcessBuilder.start`) from the deserialization of the document.
candidates.title: Unrestricted polymorphic deserialization in XStream 1.4.6 (no type allowlist) enables remote code execution via default dynamic-proxy/JDK gadget path
candidates.trace: 1. `XStream.fromXML(String)` (XStream.java:1002) → `unmarshal(Reader,...)` (XStream.java:1155-1166) → `TreeMarshallingStrategy` → `TreeUnmarshaller.start()` (TreeUnmarshaller.java:131-141) → `HierarchicalStreams.readClassType(reader, mapper)` (HierarchicalStreams.java:25-34) → `mapper.realClass(nodeName)`. 2. `DefaultMapper.realClass` (DefaultMapper.java:63-81) executes `Class.forName(elementName, initialize, classLoader)` on the attacker-supplied name with initialization enabled for non-array names, so arbitrary classes are loaded/initialized and no allowlist is consulted. 3. A `dynamic-proxy` element resolves to `DynamicProxy.class` via the default `DynamicProxyMapper` (XStream.java:567); `DynamicProxyConverter.unmarshal` (DynamicProxyConverter.java:100-135) resolves each `interface` value and the `handler class` attribute through `mapper.realClass` and calls `Proxy.newProxyInstance(..., interfacesAsArray, handler)` with the attacker-chosen `InvocationHandler` type; `context.convertAnother(proxy, handlerType)` then instantiates that handler and fills its fields from the document through the reflection converter (type-from-class-attribute at AbstractReflectionConverter.java:331-337; `instantiateNewInstance` at 542-555; default `ReflectionConverter`/`SerializableConverter`/`ExternalizableConverter` registration at XStream.java:748-754). 4. During unmarshalling, `TreeSetConverter.unmarshal` (TreeSetConverter.java:58-97) populates a `TreeSet` (and `TreeMapConverter` likewise) with attacker-supplied elements/comparator, so element/comparator methods (e.g. `compareTo`) are invoked on the dynamic proxy while the document is still being read. 5. The proxy dispatches that call into the populated `InvocationHandler`; with a JDK `java.beans.EventHandler` handler whose `target`/`action` fields were set from the document, the invoked action executes a method on the attacker-chosen target object (e.g. `java.lang.ProcessBuilder.start`), yielding command execution as a side effect of deserialization. The same unrestricted class resolution is also reachable through the Java-serialization-based converters (`SerializableConverter`, `ExternalizableConverter`, `CustomObjectInputStream.resolveClass`, core/util/CustomObjectInputStream.java:105-113) and through `resolves-to`/`defined-in` attributes.
candidates.unverified: The end-to-end RCE was not executed or runtime-confirmed and no test suite exists in the snapshot; the final trigger step depends on the JDK version/classpath providing a suitable `InvocationHandler` gadget (JDK `java.beans.EventHandler` is assumed but not verified in this environment). XStream is a deserialization library, so an application may already avoid unmarshalling untrusted data; the finding assumes the common pattern of parsing attacker-influenced documents. Parser-level details of the bundled Xpp3 driver and the exact JDK internal behavior of the gadget classes were not inspectable from this tree.
candidates.weakness_type: Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) / unsafe polymorphic deserialization leading to remote code execution

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot (406 visible, non-binary source/text files; no sensitive-name or symlink exclusions reported). Enumerated the whole tree and focused deep reading on the deserialization pipeline: `XStream` (mapper chain, converter registration, fromXML/unmarshal), `TreeUnmarshaller`, `HierarchicalStreams`, `DefaultMapper` and the other mappers, `AbstractReflectionConverter`/`ReflectionConverter`, `SerializableConverter`, `ExternalizableConverter`, `CustomObjectInputStream`/`CustomObjectOutputStream`, `DynamicProxyConverter`, collection converters (`TreeSetConverter`, `TreeMapConverter`), the XML/JSON drivers (Dom, Stax/StandardStax, Xpp, Dom4J, JDOM, XOM, Jettison), `XStreamer`, and the persistence package; also sampled the benchmark and Hibernate modules. Ran targeted searches for exec/file/network/reflection/parser patterns (`Runtime.getRuntime`, `ProcessBuilder`, `Class.forName`, `DocumentBuilderFactory`, `XMLInputFactory`, `setFeature`, `SUPPORT_DTD`, `new File`, `openConnection`, `TransformerFactory`, `ScriptEngine`) and for any security/allowlist machinery (`TypePermission`, `allowTypes`, `security`), which is absent. Repository-provided docs/build files were treated as untrusted data; no external services, patches, or runtime execution were used.
limitations: Static read-only review: nothing was compiled, executed, or run under a debugger; the RCE chain (and the XXE lead) is not runtime-confirmed.
The snapshot contains no test suite or dependency jars, so bundled parser behavior (e.g. Xpp3 MXParser entity handling) and exact gadget behavior on a specific JDK could not be verified.

Not every one of the 406 files was read line-by-line; large less security-relevant files (e.g. AbstractJsonWriter, CGLIBEnhancedConverter, BJDom4J/XOM readers, benchmark code) were sampled or searched rather than fully audited, so an independent issue there cannot be excluded.

Version identified from pom.xml/changes.html as 1.4.6; if a deployment adds custom mappers/converters or an external allowlist, exposure would change, but the library itself offers no such mechanism in this snapshot.
The final RCE trigger relies on JDK-provided gadget classes that are not defined in this repository, so gadget availability is an environment assumption.

rejected_leads.lead: Unhardened XML parsers in DOM/StAX drivers (XXE): `DomDriver` creates a plain `DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance()` (xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/io/xml/DomDriver.java:64) and `StaxDriver.createInputFactory()`/`StandardStaxDriver.createInputFactory()` return default `XMLInputFactory` instances (StaxDriver.java:240-242; StandardStaxDriver.java:73-90) with no `disallow-doctype-decl`, `setExpandEntityReferences(false)`, `SUPPORT_DTD=false` or `IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false`; no `setFeature` XXE hardening exists anywhere in the tree.
rejected_leads.reason: This is a real hardening gap (the later CVE-2016-3674 class), but it requires the application to select a DOM/StAX driver (the default `new XStream()` uses XppDriver), and its impact is typically local file disclosure/SSRF rather than code execution. It is a different root cause from the selected candidate, which is more severe, so it is recorded as a rejected secondary lead rather than a second candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Native Java deserialization embedded in `XStreamer.fromXML` (xstream/src/java/com/thoughtworks/xstream/XStreamer.java:148-163): the document carries a serialized XStream configuration that is read with `ObjectInputStream` (`configIn.readObject()`), an even more direct arbitrary-deserialization path.
rejected_leads.reason: Same unsafe-deserialization theme as the selected candidate and only reachable when an application deliberately uses `XStreamer` on untrusted data; treated as part of the same root cause rather than a separate finding.

rejected_leads.lead: Path handling in `FilePersistenceStrategy`/`AbstractFilePersistenceStrategy` (FilePersistenceStrategy.java:127-157, AbstractFilePersistenceStrategy.java:157-214): keys become file names under the base directory.
rejected_leads.reason: Inspected the escaping logic: `/`, `\` and `%` are in the default illegal-character set and are percent-escaped, so a straightforward traversal on write was not confirmed; the remainder (NPE if the base path is not a directory at lines 91/192) is robustness, not a security issue.
Only enables ReDoS inside the application's own use of the resulting pattern; no evidence of a library-level security impact on its own.

summary: The snapshot is the full XStream 1.4.6 source tree (pom.xml version 1.4.6, changes.html ends at the 1.4.6 release). The strongest source-supported issue is that this version has no type allow/deny mechanism at all: every XML element/attribute name or `class` attribute can be turned into an arbitrary class via `DefaultMapper.realClass()` → `Class.forName(...)`, the default mapper chain registers the dynamic-proxy mapper/converter, and reflection/serialization converters instantiate and populate attacker-chosen classes. The default converter set plus collection converters that invoke element/comparator methods during unmarshalling give a complete deserialization-to-code-execution path using JDK-provided gadget types (e.g. `java.beans.EventHandler` as `InvocationHandler` pointing at `java.lang.ProcessBuilder`), which is the CVE-2013-7285 class of vulnerability fixed only by the 1.4.7 security framework that is absent here. A secondary, lower-impact hardening gap (unhardened DOM/StAX parsers → XXE) was also found but rejected in favor of the RCE candidate; the candidate is a static-analysis lead and was not executed or runtime-confirmed.
